papers.title_in_file: Solving Large-Scale QUBO with Transferred Parameters from Multilevel QAOA of low depth
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, method overview, experiment discussion, conclusion
papers.what_it_is: A multilevel QAOA solver for large QUBO problems that transfers low-depth QAOA parameters from the coarsest level to finer levels and adds genetic algorithms.

assertions.value: The authors report that they numerically observe that, for p = 1 circuits, the optimal QAOA parameters are approximately transferred between circuits at different levels of the multilevel hierarchy.
quotes: we numerically observe that for p = 1 circuits, the optimal parameters are approximately transferred between the circuits at different levels of the hierarchy
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical observation in one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that, within the multilevel setting, their quantum solver outperforms Burer-Monteiro roughly half the time, and they anticipate that increasing the QAOA depth would further enhance solution quality.
quotes: within the multilevel setting, we observe that our quantum solver outperforms Burer-Monteiro roughly half the time
We anticipate that increasing the QAOA depth would further enhance solution quality.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; the depth statement is an anticipation.
assertions.reader_inference: The solver runs on the analytic p = 1 QAOA form, so this is a simulated, not hardware, comparison.

assertions.value: The authors state that they apply Quantum Relax & Round only in the p = 1 QAOA regime, where analytic expressions for spin correlations are available, because collecting extensive samples for large-scale problems remains infeasible.
quotes: we employ QRR specifically for the p = 1 QAOA regime, where analytic expressions for spin correlations are available [9]
collecting extensive samples for largescale problems remains infeasible
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope in Section III.

assertions.value: The authors list as open that the parameter transfer is not proved analytically for p = 1 QAOA+QRR in the multilevel setup, and that performance at higher circuit depth is not investigated.
quotes: proving the parameter transfer analytically for p = 1 QAOA+QRR within the multilevel setup for toy problems
investigating the performance of our method for higher circuit depth
assertions.certainty_reason: Conclusion lists these as open directions.

papers.title_in_file: An Improved Classical Singular Value Transformation for Quantum Machine Learning
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v4 (28 Jul 2024); record id says 2024, folder says 2023.
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction and results, discussion section on speedups and open problems; proofs not read
papers.what_it_is: A classical quantum-inspired algorithm that simulates QSVT on low-rank classical data with a small polynomial overhead, improving prior dequantization results.

assertions.value: The authors state that they provide a classical algorithm that matches the performance of QSVT in the low-rank regime up to a small polynomial overhead, challenging QML speedup proposals.
quotes: We challenge these proposals by providing a classical algorithm that matches the performance of QSVT in this regime up to a small polynomial overhead.
assertions.certainty_reason: Main theorem, proved in the paper (abstract and Section 1.1).
assertions.reader_inference: The regime is classical low-rank input with linear-time preprocessing, so this does not rule out speedups elsewhere.

assertions.value: The authors state that, instantiating the algorithm with different polynomials, they improve on prior classical algorithms for quantum-inspired regression, recommendation systems and Hamiltonian simulation.
quotes: we improve on prior classical algorithms for quantum-inspired regression [CGLLTW22; GST22], recommendation systems [Tan19; CGLLTW22], and Hamiltonian simulation [CGLLTW22]
assertions.certainty_reason: Corollaries 1.2, 1.4 and 1.6 (formal versions in Section 10).

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum-inspired linear algebra crucially relies on the input data being classical, so dequantization results do not apply when data is given as a quantum state.
assertions.anchor: Section 3, Discussion: Speedups in quantum machine learning
quotes: quantum-inspired linear algebra crucially relies on the input data being classical, meaning that, for example, we are given input data as a list of entries, rather than as a quantum state
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit of its own result in the Discussion.

assertions.value: The authors state that algorithms can resist dequantization by using high-degree sparsity-based QSVT rather than low-rank-based QSVT, because their techniques do not extend to that regime, and that sparsity-based QSVT is BQP-complete.
quotes: Even given classical data, algorithms can resist dequantization by using high-degree sparsitybased QSVT rather than low-rank-based QSVT, as techniques do not extend to this regime.
sparsity-based QSVT is BQP-complete
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its technique in Section 3.

papers.title_in_file: Learning quantum Hamiltonians at any temperature in polynomial time
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v2 (8 May 2026); filename and folder say 2023.
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, motivation, technical overview discussion and open questions; proofs not read
papers.what_it_is: A polynomial-time algorithm for learning a local Hamiltonian from copies of its Gibbs state at any constant inverse temperature, based on a sum-of-squares relaxation.

assertions.value: The authors state that they fully resolve the open problem of efficient Hamiltonian learning, giving a polynomial time algorithm from polynomially many copies of the Gibbs state at any constant inverse temperature.
quotes: We fully resolve this problem, giving a polynomial time algorithm for learning
assertions.certainty_reason: Main theorem, Section 1.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that prior work resolved efficient learning only in the limited cases of high temperature or commuting terms, and that the earlier algorithm by Anshu et al. used only polynomially many copies but took exponential time.
quotes: with prior work only resolving this in the limited cases of high temperature [HKT22] or commuting terms [AAKS21]
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result about other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that improving their doubly exponential dependence to singly exponential is an interesting open question.
quotes: It is an interesting open question to improve our doubly exponential dependence to singly exponential.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states a limit of its own result in a footnote, p.3.
assertions.reader_inference: The polynomial running time holds for constant inverse temperature and does not remove this dependence.

papers.what_it_is: A proposal and simulation of a continuous-variable quantum Boltzmann machine for photonic hardware that generates continuous distributions from classical (SAR image) and quantum data.

assertions.value: The authors report that their CVQBM obtained high fidelity and low Kuller-Leibler divergence, and state that it learns distributions from given data well.
quotes: We obtained high fidelity and low Kuller-Leibler (KL) divergence showing that our CVQBM learns distributions from given data well
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated result from one study on SAR image and quantum data.
assertions.reader_inference: No classical baseline comparison is stated in the abstract.

assertions.value: The authors state that the experiments were conducted on a simulator, and that currently available cloud photonic hardware cannot accommodate the CVQBM, so the hardware realization is left to future work.
quotes: Even though experiments were conducted on a simulator, we discuss experimental feasibility of our simulations
We leave the experimental realization of our CVQBM model on photonic quantum hardware to future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states its own scope in the Introduction and Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Xanadu X-series cannot accommodate the CVQBM mainly because of the lack of online squeezers, since the parameters of the available offline squeezers are fixed.
quotes: cannot accommodate our CVQBM mainly due to the lack of online squeezers (the parameters of the available offline squeezers are fixed)
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper states the limit in Section 5.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Machine Learning for Malware Classification
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, dataset section, QNN discussion excerpts, conclusion; appendix tables not read
papers.what_it_is: An exploratory comparison of QSVM and QNN models with classical models for classifying malicious and benign executable files on two datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QNN never gives better results than the classical NN, though its performance gets close when optimized, and that the QSVM gives for some parameters better results than several classical SVM on a quantum simulator.
quotes: the QNN never gives better results than the classical NN, even if its performances get close to the performances of the classical model when we optimize it
gives for some parameters better results than several classical SVM when computed on quantum simulator
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one exploratory study.

assertions.value: The authors report that extracting the most impactful features gave much better results than the Grayscale image method for each model.
quotes: the preprocessing consisting in extracting the
most impactful features gave much better results than the Grayscale method
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that their work is exploratory, and that the classical neural network used a naive batch size for the comparison, which they say is not realistic.
quotes: Our work here is exploratory
We know that it is not realistic to take such a batch-size for a classical neural network
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope and comparison setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The QNN against classical NN comparison is therefore weak evidence about relative merit.

papers.title_in_file: Ansatz-Agnostic Exponential Resource Saving in Variational Quantum Algorithms Using Shallow Shadows
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, theorem statements, barren plateau discussion, conclusion; proofs not read
papers.what_it_is: AISO, a shallow-shadow training protocol that cuts the quantum resources of variational algorithm training for almost any shallow ansatz with low-Frobenius-norm observables.

assertions.value: The authors state that their protocol based on shallow shadows achieves similar levels of savings for almost any shallow ansatz studied in the literature, when combined with observables of low Frobenius norm.
quotes: we present a protocol based on shallow shadows that achieves similar levels of savings for almost any shallow ansatz studied in the literature, when combined with observables of low Frobenius norm
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 3 and Theorem 4 give the sample cost.

assertions.value: The authors state that they experimentally demonstrate orders of magnitude improvement in comparison to the standard VQA model.
quotes: We also experimentally demonstrate orders of magnitude improvement in comparison to the standard VQA model.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Figures are in the simulation section, not read here.

assertions.value: The authors state that the protocol is shown compatible with variational quantum state preparation and variational quantum circuit synthesis, and that its scope is shallow ansatzes with observables of low Frobenius norm.
quotes: variational quantum state preparation and variational quantum circuit synthesis, are compatible with our protocol
almost any shallow ansatz and observables with low Frobenius norm
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope in the abstract and conclusion.

papers.title_in_file: Combinatorial optimization with quantum imaginary time evolution
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, conclusion; methods and result tables not read
papers.what_it_is: A numerical study of QITE with linear and entangling ansatzes on PUBO problems, namely weighted MaxCut and LABS.

assertions.value: The authors report that QITE with a separable ansatz often outperforms the Goemans-Williamson algorithm on weighted MaxCut on graphs up to 150 vertices.
quotes: On weighted MaxCut, QITE with a separable Ansatz often outperforms the GW algorithm on graphs up to 150 vertices.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulation study.

assertions.value: The authors report that QITE on the LABS problem with a separable ansatz is comparable with p = 10 QAOA, and that they do not see a significant advantage with an entangling ansatz.
quotes: We find the performance of QITE on the LABS problem with a separable Ansatz comparable with p = 10 QAOA, and do not see a significant advantage with an entangling Ansatz.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that their separable ansatz can be simulated efficiently classically, and that their results indicate much larger graphs are needed to observe quantum advantage.
quotes: Our separable Ansatz can be simulated efficiently classically.
Our results indicate that much larger graphs are needed to be considered in order to observe quantum advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit of its own method in the Conclusion.
assertions.reader_inference: The reported outperformance of GW is therefore not evidence of a quantum advantage.

papers.title_in_file: Solving Power Grid Optimization Problems with Rydberg Atoms
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, conclusion; methods and figures not read
papers.what_it_is: MaxCut formulations of power grid problems solved with an optimized adiabatic pulse and a local-detuning QAOA on neutral-atom hardware (QuEra Aquila) and simulators.

assertions.value: The authors report that, with under 100 embedding steps, the adiabatic algorithm found the ground state with over 95% overlap, and that they found an average 60% overlap with the ground state experimentally on the Aquila processor.
quotes: We found that with under 100 embedding steps, the adiabatic algorithm was able to find the ground state with over 95% overlap.
we found an average 60% overlap with the ground state experimentally
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; the 95% figure is from simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that with the Adam optimizer and up to 10 QAOA layers they found the MaxCut on average with probability ranging from 67% (for 10 vertices) to 50% (for 13 vertices).
quotes: Using the Adam Optimizer for the classical optimization and up to 10 QAOA layers we were able to find
the MaxCut on average with probability ranging from 67% (for 10 vertices) to 50% (for 13 vertices).
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that their optimization was performed on a simulator instead of the Aquila hardware, and describe the hardware performance as far from ideal though adequate to yield the solution.
quotes: Since our optimization was performed on a simulator instead of the Aquila hardware, it is important to study the performance when the optimization is performed on actual hardware.
Although far from ideal, the performance of the QuEra processor was adequate to yield the solution to the problem at hand.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit in the Conclusion.
